newsitem.title: CANADA: CWB boosts wheat, barley output outlook, cut durum.
newsitem.headline: CWB boosts wheat, barley output outlook, cut durum.

text.p: Canadian spring wheat yield estimates were revised upward to the five-year average, a Canadian Wheat Board analyst said.
"We got those rains in the area that was dry so we bumped up our yield estimates on wheat," said Paul Bullock, director of weather and crop surveillance at the CWB.
Spring wheat yields were expected to range from 30 to 32 bushels an acre, the five-year average, due to timely rains at the end of June and first week of July, Bullock said.
The CWB previously, on June 11 had forecast spring wheat yield estimates at 29.5 to 31.5 bushels per acre. That forecast was linked to drought conditions on southeast Prairies at that time.
Barley output was expected to exceed trend yields of 55 bushels an acre, possibly into the "high 50s" due to the rains, but Bullock declined to provide a specific estimate.

Durum wheat output, however, was expected to fall short of the five-year average of 30 bushels per acre as rain fell too late on some drought-stricken fields in southeastern Saskatchewan to significantly aid the crop, he said.

"There's crop down in the Weyburn area that just isn't going to recover no matter how much rain you give it," Bullock said. "It just got hurt too badly. It may not be as bad as it started off but we don't think it'll come back to average."
Cereal quality may be an issue once the crop is harvested after the southeastern Prairies saw dry conditions from April to June and the northwestern Prairies saw excess rain.
"But I'd say half the Prairies are in average to above average condition with generally favourable moisture conditions," Bullock said.
Cereal crops were now advanced far enough in their growth for the focus of attention to shift to pest and disease threats to yield rather than on moisture levels, he added.
Cereals will be heading in the next two to three weeks and will be vulnerable to heading diseases, he said.
